full_description:
Description: Chunky little brown bird hopping around the cafe tables looking for crumbs. The male had a grey cap, chestnut-brown sides to the head, a black bib under the beak and pale grey cheeks. Thick stubby beak. A whole noisy gang of them was chirping in the hedge.
Location: Outdoor cafe, Delhi, India (winter)
reasoning: The description of a chunky little brown bird with a grey cap, chestnut-brown sides to the head, black bib, pale grey cheeks, and thick stubby beak seen in a noisy gang at an outdoor cafe in Delhi during winter strongly suggests a sparrow species. The key field marks are: grey cap, chestnut sides to head, black bib, pale grey cheeks, and thick stubby beak. This combination is characteristic of the House Sparrow (Passer domesticus), which is extremely common around human habitation in India, especially at cafes and outdoor eating areas. The male plumage description matches House Sparrow perfectly. Other sparrow species in India like the Eurasian Tree Sparrow (Passer montanus) have a chestnut cap (not grey) and a smaller black bib, which contradicts the description. The Spanish Sparrow (Passer hispaniolensis) is rare in India and has different plumage. The description's emphasis on the grey cap, chestnut cheeks/sides, and prominent black bib, combined with the location (outdoor cafe in Delhi) and behavior (hopping around looking for crumbs in a noisy gang), definitively points to House Sparrow.

full_description:
Description: A drake duck paddling on the canal next to a brown female, tipping tail-up to feed instead of diving.
Location: Canal, Amsterdam, Netherlands (spring)
Size and shape: Large, heavy-bodied duck
Colour patterns: Shiny bottle-green head, thin white collar, chestnut chest, grey body, little curled black feathers on the tail, blue wing patch edged in white
Beak type: Flat, yellow
Foot type: Orange, webbed
reasoning: The description matches a male Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) perfectly: shiny bottle-green head, thin white collar, chestnut chest, grey body, curled black tail feathers, blue speculum edged in white, yellow bill, orange feet, and the characteristic tail-up dabbling feeding behavior. The location (Amsterdam canal) and season (spring) are consistent with Mallards. The presence of a brown female nearby further supports this, as female Mallards are brown and often found with drakes. Other dabbling ducks with green heads (like Northern Pintail or Eurasian Wigeon) lack the combination of chestnut chest, white collar, and grey body. The blue speculum edged in white is diagnostic for Mallard among European dabbling ducks. No similar species remain after applying these field marks.

full_description:
Description: The usual city pigeon: plump grey bird with a small head, two black bars across each wing, a white patch on the rump when it flew, and green and purple shine on the neck. Walking around bobbing its head and pecking at bread near the station.
Location: Station square, Milan, Italy (all year)
reasoning: The description matches the Rock Pigeon (Columba livia), which is the common city pigeon found throughout Europe including Milan. The key field marks mentioned—plump grey body, small head, two black bars on wings, white rump patch, and iridescent green and purple neck sheen—are all diagnostic of Rock Pigeon. The behavior (head-bobbing, pecking at bread) and habitat (urban station) are typical. No other pigeon species commonly found in Milan year-round matches this combination of features. The white rump patch and wing bars specifically distinguish it from other European pigeons like the Wood Pigeon (which has white neck patches and lacks the wing bars) or Stock Dove (which lacks the white rump and has different neck coloring).

full_description:
Description: Small round bird with a bright orange-red face and breast edged with blue-grey, a brown back and a white belly. Big dark eye and a thin beak. It followed me while I was digging and perched on the spade handle.
Location: Back garden, Manchester, UK (winter)
reasoning: The description of a small round bird with bright orange-red face and breast, blue-grey edging, brown back, white belly, dark eye, and thin beak is characteristic of a European Robin. The behavior of following a person digging and perching on a spade handle is typical robin behavior. In Manchester, UK during winter, this is a common resident species. No other British garden bird matches this combination of features: the orange-red face and breast are diagnostic for Robin. Redstarts have orange-red breasts but lack the orange face and are summer visitors. Bullfinches have red breasts but have black caps and are much less likely to approach humans. The description rules out all similar species through the combination of orange-red face (not just breast), the blue-grey edging, and the behavioral context of a winter garden visitor in the UK.

full_description:
Description: Fairly big songbird, much bigger than a sparrow, running across the lawn, stopping with its head tilted, then pulling up an earthworm. Brick-orange breast, dark grey back, almost black head with a broken white ring around the eye, and a yellow beak.
Location: Suburban lawn, Minnesota, USA (spring)
reasoning: The description matches an American Robin very well: fairly large songbird (much bigger than a sparrow), brick-orange breast, dark grey back, distinctive head pattern with white eye-ring, yellow beak, and the characteristic behavior of running on lawns and pulling up earthworms. Other thrushes could be considered: Wood Thrush has a rusty head and spotted breast (not matching the brick-orange breast and dark head described); Hermit Thrush has a rusty tail and spotted breast (not matching); Eastern Bluebird is smaller and has a blue back (not grey); Varied Thrush has orange underparts but is western and has a black breast band (not described). The combination of size, brick-orange breast, dark grey back, almost black head with white eye-ring, yellow beak, and the earthworm-pulling behavior on a lawn in Minnesota spring is diagnostic for American Robin. No similar species remain after applying the user's specific details.

full_description:
Description: Bright red bird that comes to my sunflower feeder every morning, usually with a brownish female.
Location: Backyard, Virginia, USA (winter)
Size and shape: Medium songbird, a bit bigger than a sparrow, with a pointed crest
Colour patterns: Bright red all over with a black face mask around the beak
Beak type: Thick, cone-shaped, orange-red
Behaviours: Cracks seeds at the feeder; loud whistling song from the top of a tree
reasoning: The description of a bright red bird with a black face mask, pointed crest, thick cone-shaped orange-red beak, and a brownish female companion visiting a sunflower feeder in Virginia during winter is characteristic of the Northern Cardinal. The pointed crest, black face mask, and bright red coloration are diagnostic features. The thick, conical beak is typical of seed-cracking cardinals. The loud whistling song and behavior at feeders match Northern Cardinal perfectly. The presence of a brownish female is consistent with sexual dimorphism in cardinals. No other common Virginia songbird matches this combination of features: Scarlet Tanagers lack the crest and black mask, House Finches lack the prominent crest and black face mask, and Red-winged Blackbirds are different in shape and lack the crest. The winter location and feeder behavior confirm this is not a migratory tanager. This description rules out all similar species.

full_description:
Description: Loud, bold bird screaming 'jay! jay!' at the feeder and stuffing peanuts into its throat. Bright blue back and wings with black bars and white spots, a blue crest, greyish-white underneath and a black necklace around the throat.
Location: Garden, New Jersey, USA (autumn)
reasoning: The description matches a Blue Jay perfectly: loud, bold behavior with characteristic 'jay' calls, eating peanuts at feeders, bright blue back and wings with black barring and white spots, blue crest, greyish-white underparts, and distinctive black necklace marking around the throat. All these field marks are diagnostic for Blue Jay. No other North American jay species has this exact combination of features, particularly the blue crest, the specific pattern of black barring on blue wings, and the black necklace marking. Steller's Jay has a crest but is found in western North America, not New Jersey. Gray Jay lacks the blue coloring entirely. No other species fits this description.

full_description:
Description: Lots of slim birds zooming low over the field catching flies. Glossy dark blue back, rusty-red throat and forehead, creamy underneath, and really long forked tails with thin streamers. They kept landing on the barn roof and twittering.
Location: Farm, Normandy, France (summer)
reasoning: The description of slim birds with glossy dark blue backs, rusty-red throats and foreheads, creamy undersides, and long forked tails with thin streamers catching flies low over a field in summer in Normandy strongly suggests swallows. The key features match Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica) very well: dark blue-black upperparts, rufous-red forehead and throat, pale underparts, and distinctively long forked tail with streamers. The behavior of catching flies in flight, landing on barn roofs, and twittering also fits Barn Swallow perfectly. Other European swallows like Sand Martin (Riparia riparia) lack the rufous throat and forehead, and have brown rather than blue backs. Cliff Swallow (Petrochelidon pyrrhonota) is a vagrant to Europe and has a different pattern. Red-rumped Swallow (Cecropis daurica) has a red rump and different throat pattern. The description's specific mention of 'rusty-red throat and forehead' combined with 'glossy dark blue back' and 'really long forked tails with thin streamers' is diagnostic for Barn Swallow. No other European swallow matches all these features together.

full_description:

Location: River, Oxfordshire, UK (autumn)

Colour patterns: Electric blue-turquoise back, orange chest and belly, orange cheek, white throat and neck patch
Beak type: Long, straight, dagger-like, black

The key field marks all align: electric blue-turquoise back, orange-red underparts, white throat patch, long straight black dagger-like bill, tiny red feet, sparrow-sized but chunky build with big head and short tail, and the characteristic behaviour of plunging into water for fish. No other UK bird species matches this combination of features. Other kingfisher species (Belted Kingfisher, Pied Kingfisher) do not occur in the UK. No other small UK bird has this coloration pattern or behaviour.

full_description:
Description: Big black-and-white bird with a really long tail, strutting on the grass. Black head and chest, bright white belly and white shoulder patches, and in the sun the wings and tail shone blue and green. It gave a loud chattering 'chak-chak-chak' when the cat came out.
Location: Suburban garden, Stockholm, Sweden (winter)
reasoning: The description of a large black-and-white bird with a long tail, iridescent blue-green wings and tail, white belly, black head and chest, white shoulder patches, and loud chattering call in suburban Stockholm strongly suggests a Eurasian Magpie (Pica pica). This species is common year-round in Sweden and matches all the described features: the distinctive black-and-white plumage with white shoulder patches, the long graduated tail that shows iridescent blue-green in sunlight, the loud 'chak-chak-chak' alarm call, and the behavior of strutting on grass. Other large black-and-white birds in Sweden (like Hooded Crow or Great Spotted Woodpecker) lack the long tail, the iridescent coloring, the white shoulder patches, or the specific call described. No other species fits all these details as well as Eurasian Magpie.

full_description:
Description: Brown bird about the size of a thrush, walking (not hopping) around the car park. Black head, chocolate-brown body, a bare bright yellow patch of skin behind the eye, yellow beak and yellow legs. Big white patches flashed on the wings when it flew. Very noisy, squawking and chattering in pairs.
Location: Car park, Mumbai, India (all year)
reasoning: The description of a brown bird with black head, chocolate-brown body, bright yellow bare skin patch behind the eye, yellow beak, yellow legs, white wing patches, and noisy behavior in pairs from Mumbai, India strongly suggests the Yellow-billed Babbler (Turdoides affinis). This species is common in Mumbai year-round, walks rather than hops, has the distinctive yellow orbital patch, yellow bill and legs, and shows white on the wings in flight. The noisy, chattering behavior in pairs is typical of babblers. Other brown babblers in India like the Large Grey Babbler (Turdoides malcolmi) lack the black head and yellow facial patch. The Jungle Babbler (Turdoides striatus) is smaller and lacks the prominent yellow orbital patch. The size comparison to a thrush, the specific color pattern (black head with chocolate-brown body), the bare yellow patch behind the eye, and the white wing patches all match Yellow-billed Babbler perfectly and rule out other similar species in the region.

full_description:
Description: Common garden bird; a pair came to eat the papaya I left out.
Location: Home garden, Lucknow, India (summer)
Size and shape: About as big as a myna but slimmer, with a short crest
Colour patterns: Black head, smoky-brown body with a scaly pattern, white rump, bright red patch under the tail
Beak type: Short, black
Behaviours: Perky, flits from bush to bush, cheerful 'be-quick-quick' call
reasoning: The description points to a crested bird with black head, smoky-brown scaly body, white rump, and bright red under-tail coverts. The size comparison to a myna, short crest, and the distinctive 'be-quick-quick' call are key. In Lucknow, India during summer, this matches the Red-vented Bulbul (Pycnonotus cafer), a very common garden bird. The white rump and red under-tail patch are diagnostic. Other bulbuls in the region like the White-eared Bulbul (Pycnonotus leucotis) lack the red under-tail and have white ear patches. The Red-whiskered Bulbul (Pycnonotus jocosus) has a crest but lacks the white rump and has red ear patches instead. The Black-headed Bulbul (Brachypodius melanocephalus) is found further east and lacks the white rump. The description's emphasis on the white rump combined with the bright red under-tail patch, black head, and scaly brown body, along with the characteristic call and behaviour, confidently identifies this as Red-vented Bulbul.

full_description:
Description: Large dark brown bird of prey circling over the rubbish dump with dozens of others, twisting its tail to steer. The tail had a shallow notch in it and the wings were long and angled. Some swooped down and grabbed scraps right off the ground. Paler head, yellow feet.
Location: City outskirts, Delhi, India (winter)
reasoning: The description fits a large dark brown raptor with a paler head, yellow feet, and long angled wings circling over a dump with others. The shallow notch in the tail and the behavior of swooping to grab scraps from the ground are key details. This matches the Indian Vulture (Gyps indicus), which is common around dumps in India and has these characteristics. The Egyptian Vulture (Neophron percnopterus) is also found in India but is much smaller and has a distinctive white body with black flight feathers, which contradicts the 'large dark brown' description. The White-rumped Vulture (Gyps bengalensis) is similar to Indian Vulture but is now extremely rare in India due to population collapse. The Himalayan Vulture (Gyps himalayanus) is larger and paler overall. The description of 'large dark brown' with 'paler head' and the behavior of feeding on scraps at dumps strongly indicates Indian Vulture. The shallow notch in the tail and long angled wings are consistent with Gyps species. No other large raptors in the region match this combination of features and behavior.

full_description:
Description: Huge dark brown eagle with a pure white head and white tail, perched on a dead tree by the river. Massive hooked yellow beak and yellow feet. It dropped down and snatched a fish off the surface.
Location: Riverside, Alaska, USA (summer)
reasoning: The description of a huge dark brown eagle with a pure white head and white tail, massive hooked yellow beak, yellow feet, and fish-catching behavior is characteristic of the Bald Eagle. This is the only North American eagle with this exact combination of features: white head and tail contrasting with dark brown body, large yellow beak and cere, yellow feet, and fish-hunting behavior. Other large raptors like Golden Eagles lack the white head and tail. Steller's Sea-Eagle has similar coloring but is not found in Alaska in summer and has different proportions. The location (Alaska riverside in summer) and behavior (fishing from a perch) are typical for Bald Eagles. No other species fits all these details together.

full_description:
Description: Tall grey wading bird standing like a statue in the marsh, then stabbing a fish.
Location: Marsh, Florida, USA (winter)
Size and shape: Very tall, over a metre, long legs and a long S-shaped neck
Wing type: Huge, broad wings; slow flight with the neck tucked back
Colour patterns: Blue-grey body, white face with a black stripe over the eye ending in plumes, rusty-brown thighs
Beak type: Long, dagger-like, yellowish
Foot type: Long dark legs
reasoning: The description of a very tall (over 1 metre), blue-grey wading bird with an S-shaped neck, long dagger-like yellowish beak, white face with black eye stripe and plumes, rusty-brown thighs, and long dark legs in a Florida marsh in winter strongly suggests a Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias). The key field marks match: the blue-grey plumage, white face with black supercilium extending into plumes, chestnut thighs, yellow bill, and the characteristic hunting posture and behaviour. Other tall grey herons in Florida include the Tricolored Heron and Little Blue Heron, but these are much smaller (not over a metre tall) and lack the white face and black eye stripe pattern described. The Sandhill Crane is also very tall but is found in Florida marshes primarily during winter migration and has a different body shape, red face, and different plumage pattern. The description's emphasis on the white face with black stripe, the rusty thighs, the size (over a metre), and the blue-grey body all point definitively to Great Blue Heron. No similar species remain after applying these specific field marks.

full_description:
Description: Tall grey heron standing in the shallows. Grey back, white crown, neck and face, a black stripe from the eye back into a thin black crest, black streaks down the front of the neck and a yellow dagger bill. When it flew it pulled its neck in and had big slow wingbeats with black flight feathers.
Location: Lake, Netherlands (winter)
reasoning: The description matches a Grey Heron (Ardea cinerea), which is common in the Netherlands year-round and especially in winter. The key field marks are: tall grey heron, grey back, white crown and neck, black stripe from eye to crest, black streaks down neck front, yellow bill, and black flight feathers with slow wingbeats and retracted neck in flight. These features are diagnostic for Grey Heron. Other European herons could be considered: Purple Heron (Ardea purpurea) has a darker, more rufous neck and is rare in winter Netherlands; Great White Egret (Ardea alba) is white overall, not grey-backed; Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) is much smaller and stockier with a different head pattern; Squacco Heron (Ardeola ralloides) is small and buff-colored. The grey back, white crown, black crest stripe, and large size rule out all alternatives. The location (Netherlands) and season (winter) support Grey Heron as a resident species.

full_description:
Description: Tiny wader, about sparrow-sized, running around the mudflats with a flock of stints. What stood out was the bill: black and flattened into a little spoon at the tip. Rusty-red head and breast. It swept its bill side to side through the mud.
Location: Mudflats, Rudong, Jiangsu, China (May, spring migration)
app_species: Red Phalarope (Phalaropus fulicarius); Red-necked Phalarope (Phalaropus lobatus)
reasoning: The description of a tiny wader with a spoon-shaped bill, rusty-red head and breast, sweeping its bill side-to-side through mud, seen on mudflats in Jiangsu in May, strongly suggests a phalarope. The spoon-shaped bill is diagnostic for phalaropes. The rusty coloration and side-to-side feeding behavior fit Red Phalarope (Phalaropus fulicarius) or Red-necked Phalarope (Phalaropus lobatus). Both species occur in East Asia during migration. Red Phalarope has a more uniformly rusty head and breast in breeding plumage, while Red-necked Phalarope has rusty coloring mainly on the neck and upper breast with a white face. The description emphasizes the rusty-red head AND breast, which fits Red Phalarope better. However, Red-necked Phalarope is more commonly encountered during spring migration in China. The 'rusty-red head and breast' could fit either species depending on plumage stage. Given the location (Jiangsu mudflats) and timing (May spring migration), both are possible, but Red-necked Phalarope is more frequently recorded. The spoon-shaped bill and side-to-side feeding behavior rule out stints and other small waders. The description is consistent with a phalarope in breeding or transitional plumage, but the exact species cannot be definitively determined from the coloration description alone without seeing the face pattern more clearly.

Description: Little black-and-white woodpecker on my suet feeder, about sparrow-sized. White stripe down the middle of the back, black wings with white spots, a small red patch on the back of the head. The beak was really short, much shorter than its head. Black spots on the white outer tail feathers.
Location: Backyard, Ohio, USA (winter)
reasoning: The description of a small black-and-white woodpecker with a white stripe down the back, white-spotted black wings, red patch on the back of the head, very short beak, and spotted outer tail feathers in Ohio during winter points strongly to Downy Woodpecker. The key field marks match: the white back stripe, black wings with white spots, red undertail coverts (or red patch on back of head in males), and the characteristically short bill. Hairy Woodpecker is a look-alike but is larger and has a longer bill relative to head size—the user specifically noted the beak was 'really short, much shorter than its head,' which rules out Hairy. Nuttall's Woodpecker and Ladder-backed Woodpecker are western species not found in Ohio. Pileated Woodpecker is much larger. The sparrow-sized description, short bill, and Ohio location all confirm Downy Woodpecker as the only remaining species.

full_description:
Description: Bold little bird hanging upside down on the peanut feeder, calling 'teacher-teacher'.
Location: Garden, Berlin, Germany (winter)
Size and shape: Sparrow-sized, a bit bigger than a blue tit
Colour patterns: Glossy black head with white cheeks, yellow belly with a thick black stripe down the middle, greenish back, blue-grey wings
Beak type: Short, pointed, black
Behaviours: Acrobatic, hangs upside down on feeders
reasoning: The description of a sparrow-sized bird with a glossy black head, white cheeks, yellow belly with a black central stripe, greenish back, and blue-grey wings, calling 'teacher-teacher' and hanging acrobatically upside down on feeders in Berlin in winter, matches the Great Tit (Parus major) very well. The 'teacher-teacher' call is diagnostic for this species. The bold black and white head pattern with white cheeks, the yellow underparts with the characteristic black stripe, and the greenish back are all field marks of Great Tit. The size (sparrow-sized, slightly larger than a Blue Tit) and acrobatic behaviour on feeders are also consistent. No other common European garden bird matches this combination of features, particularly the distinctive 'teacher-teacher' call and the specific colour pattern. The Coal Tit has a white patch on the nape but lacks the bold white cheeks and yellow belly stripe. The Blue Tit is smaller and lacks the black head and yellow belly. The Marsh Tit lacks the white cheeks and yellow belly. No other species fits all these details together in winter Berlin.

full_description:
Description: Tiny friendly bird, round and fluffy, with a black cap and black bib, bright white cheeks, grey back and buffy sides. It sang 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee' and even landed on my hand for sunflower seeds. Tiny short black beak.
Location: Nature trail, Vermont, USA (winter)
reasoning: The description of a tiny, round, fluffy bird with a black cap, black bib, white cheeks, grey back, buffy sides, and the distinctive 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee' song is characteristic of chickadees. In Vermont in winter, the most likely species is the Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus), which is common year-round and known for being friendly and visiting feeders. The Boreal Chickadee (Poecile hudsonica) is also present in Vermont but is less common and has a brown (not grey) back and rusty (not buffy) sides. The Carolina Chickadee (Poecile carolinensis) has a similar appearance but its range does not extend to Vermont. The description's mention of grey back and buffy sides, combined with the location and season, strongly indicates Black-capped Chickadee. The Boreal Chickadee can be ruled out by the grey back (Boreal has brown back) and buffy sides (Boreal has rusty sides). Carolina Chickadee is ruled out by geography—it does not occur in Vermont.

full_description:
Description: Glossy black bird with a purple and green sheen, covered in little white spots, with a short square tail and a pointed beak. Walking busily on the lawn probing the grass. At dusk huge flocks swirled around in the sky.
Location: Park, Rome, Italy (winter)
reasoning: The description of a glossy black bird with purple and green iridescent sheen, covered in white spots, short square tail, pointed beak, probing behavior on lawns, and forming huge flocking displays at dusk strongly suggests a starling. In Rome in winter, the most likely candidate is the Common Starling (Sturnus vulgaris), which is abundant and matches all these details perfectly—the white spotting is characteristic of winter plumage, the iridescent sheen is typical, the pointed beak is used for probing, and the massive murmurations (swirling flocks) at dusk are a famous behavior. The Spotless Starling (Sturnus unicolor) is resident in southern Europe but lacks the white spots entirely, so it is ruled out by the 'covered in little white spots' detail. The Rose-colored Starling (Pastor roseus) has a different color pattern (pink and black) and is not present in Rome in winter. No other species matches this combination of features.

Colour patterns: Bright metallic green back, white underneath, glowing ruby-red throat that looked black in some light

The ruby-red gorget is diagnostic for Ruby-throated Hummingbird males. The behavior of hovering at feeders and chasing others is typical. No other species common to Georgia in July matches all these details.

full_description:
Description: Big chunky kingfisher sitting on the fence: cream-white head and belly, a dark eye with a dark brown stripe through it, brown wings with pale blue spots, a rusty barred tail and a huge heavy beak. At sunrise a group of them did a loud laughing chorus, 'koo-koo-koo-ha-ha-ha'.
Location: Suburb, Brisbane, Australia (spring)
reasoning: The description matches a Kookaburra, specifically the Laughing Kookaburra (Dacelo novaeguineae), which is common in Brisbane suburbs. The key identifying features are: large chunky kingfisher, cream-white head and belly, dark eye-stripe, brown wings with pale blue spots, rusty barred tail, huge heavy beak, and the distinctive loud laughing call 'koo-koo-koo-ha-ha-ha' at dawn. This is the iconic Australian bird known for exactly this behavior and appearance. Other Australian kingfishers like the Blue-winged Kookaburra (Dacelo leachii) are found in northern Australia, not Brisbane. The Sacred Kingfisher (Todiramphus sanctus) is much smaller and lacks the chunky build and pale coloring. The Azure Kingfisher (Ceyx azurea) is also much smaller. No other kingfisher species in Australia matches this combination of large size, coloration pattern, and the characteristic laughing call. The description rules out all similar species through the combination of location (Brisbane), size (big chunky), coloration (cream-white head/belly, brown wings with pale blue spots, rusty barred tail), and especially the unmistakable laughing chorus call.

full_description:

Location: City park, Sydney, Australia (summer)
reasoning: The description matches a Rainbow Lorikeet (Trichoglossus moluccanus), which is common in Sydney parks. The key field marks are: deep blue head, bright red chest with orange, green back and wings, dark blue belly, and curved red beak. The behaviour of hanging upside down in flowering trees, screeching constantly, and moving in small flocks is typical of lorikeets. Other Australian parrots like the Sulphur-crested Cockatoo are white with yellow, the Galah is pink and grey, and the King Parrot has a different colour pattern (red head and underparts in males, green in females). The Scaly-breasted Lorikeet is smaller and lacks the deep blue head and red chest. No other common Sydney parrot matches this specific combination of colours and behaviour.

full_description:
Description: Black-and-white bird that swooped at my head while I was cycling past in spring.
Location: Bike path, Melbourne, Australia (September)
Size and shape: About crow-sized, sturdy
Colour patterns: Black face and underparts; white nape and white back; white shoulder patches and rump; black tail tip
